name: Arizona

notes: Groceries: on the November 3, 2026 ballot, Proposition 316 would from June 30, 2027 freeze city food taxes of 2% or more, let lower ones rise only by a vote and only to 2%, and require a vote for new ones (capped at 2%); no adoption or increase could take effect in the 24 months before June 30, 2027, and it would apply back to January 1, 2025.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and spirits are taxed at the full rate, on top of the state luxury tax paid by distributors ($3 a gallon on spirits, 84 cents on wine, 16 cents on beer), which is left out here.
Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the full rate, on top of the $2.00-a-pack cigarette tax and the tax on other tobacco products, left out here. No state tax on vapor products was found.
Barber and beauty services: personal services such as haircuts aren't taxed: no TPT classification covers them (no ADOR statement found that says so directly).
Laundry and dry cleaning services aren't taxed: no TPT classification covers them (no ADOR statement found that says so directly).
Motor fuel is exempt from TPT and taxed by the gallon instead: 18 cents for gasoline, left out here. A 2026 bill for a fuel tax holiday (HB 2400) was not enacted.
Repair labor billed separately from parts is not taxed.
Diapers, menstrual products and other hygiene products are taxed at the full rate; Arizona has no sales tax holiday.
Hotel stays pay city hotel taxes and, in Maricopa and Pima counties, county lodging taxes, which are not counted here.
gaps: Arizona taxes sellers (transaction privilege tax) rather than buyers; rates are passed on like a sales tax.

Groceries (food for home consumption) carry no state or county tax; each city taxes them at its own rate, which is used here, and 22 cities don't tax them (Bullhead City, Camp Verde, Flagstaff, Jerome, Kingman, Lake Havasu City, Marana, Mesa, Oro Valley, Parker, Phoenix, Quartzsite, Sahuarita, San Tan Valley, Sedona, South Tucson, Superior, Surprise, Tombstone, Tucson, Tusayan, Williams).

Restaurants and bars: 23 cities tax them at a different rate from other retail sales (Casa Grande, Chandler, Colorado City, Eloy, Flagstaff, Glendale, Goodyear, Guadalupe, Jerome, Kingman, Lake Havasu City, Page, Parker, Peoria, Pinetop-Lakeside, Quartzsite, Sierra Vista, South Tucson, Surprise, Tusayan, Williams, Winslow, Yuma); their restaurant rate is used for restaurants.

Places in two counties: a tract at least half in the city takes the city's rate with its own county's: Apache Junction (Pinal County, Maricopa County); Hayden (Gila County, Pinal County); Marana (Pima County, Pinal County); Peoria (Maricopa County, Yavapai County); Queen Creek (Maricopa County, Pinal County); Sedona (Yavapai County, Coconino County); Wickenburg (Maricopa County, Yavapai County); Winkelman (Gila County, Pinal County).
Some cities tax the part of a single item's price above a set amount at a lower rate (Phoenix 2% above $14,338, for one; 29 cities in all); not counted.
Taxes on sales on tribal lands are not counted.
San Tan Valley incorporated after the 2024 Census place list; its rate is applied to the San Tan Valley CDP.

Local sales tax votes on November 3, 2026 (Flagstaff, Tempe, Tucson's zoo tax renewal, Prescott Valley and Yavapai County) and San Tan Valley's grocery tax from January 1, 2027 are noted on those pages; the rates here are ADOR's for November 1, 2026. Smaller towns' November measures weren't all checked.

0423620: On November 3, 2026 Flagstaff voters decide on a 0.5% sales tax for public safety from July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2042, which would raise the city's rate from 2.486% to 2.986%; it wouldn't apply to groceries (City of Flagstaff, call of election). The current rate is used here.
0457450: On November 3, 2026 Prescott Valley voters decide on Proposition 493, a 0.5% sales tax for a pool and recreation center, as reported (KNAU); not confirmed on the town's own pages. The current rate is used here.
0464210: San Tan Valley, which incorporated in 2025, taxes food for home consumption at 2.25% from January 1, 2027 (Ordinance 2026-06; ADOR); groceries here are at 0% until then. If Proposition 316 passes on November 3, a new city food tax adopted without a vote, above 2% or in the 24 months before June 30, 2027 could be barred, which would reach this one (Proposition 316 applies back to January 1, 2025).
0473000: On November 3, 2026 Tempe voters decide on Proposition 424, a 0.5% sales tax for public safety, transit and early childhood programs, not on food for home consumption (City of Tempe). The current rate is used here.
0477000: On November 3, 2026 Tucson voters decide on Proposition 422, renewing the city's 0.1% zoo tax from January 1, 2028 to December 31, 2047; it is in the current rate (City of Tucson).
04025: On November 3, 2026 Yavapai County voters decide on Proposition 497, which would raise the county jail district's sales tax by 0.25% (to 0.5%, as reported by KNAU) for 20 years from July 1, 2027 (Yavapai County Elections). The current rate is used here.

programs: Arizona has no enterprise zones (the program ended in 2011, as reported). Its two Military Reuse Zones aren't mapped: no boundaries are published (ADOR). Phoenix-Mesa Gateway's was first designated in 1996 and last renewed in 2015, and Phoenix-Goodyear's was designated in 2002 and renewed for ten years in 2017 (ADOR), so whether both are still in force wasn't confirmed. Its seven foreign-trade zones (60, 75, 139, 174, 219, 221 and 277) aren't mapped either: the federal Foreign-Trade Zones Board publishes their site lists and service-area maps, not map layers.

Business improvement districts are mapped for downtown Tucson (the city's 2022 layer). Not mapped (no official map found): the enhanced municipal services districts of downtown Phoenix, Tempe (downtown and Rio Salado), Mesa and Chandler, and Flagstaff's downtown district.

Redevelopment and incentive areas aren't mapped: Phoenix's Neighborhood Services map draws about 20 redevelopment areas, but the city's current list couldn't be confirmed; Mesa's four redevelopment areas (its central business district, where GPLET abatements apply) have no published layer; Tucson's Rio Nuevo district, where a share of state sales tax growth funds development, is drawn only on a 2000 city layer.

warn.text: Scottsdale draws many visitors (resorts, spring training, Old Town), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (8.6%) and its 169 lodging places (0.7 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 24 of its 58 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of Scottsdale's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Flagstaff draws many visitors (the Grand Canyon gateway and Route 66), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (6.3%) and its 118 lodging places (1.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 7 of its 18 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of Flagstaff's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Paradise Valley's resorts draw many visitors, but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (5.3%) and its 17 lodging places (1.3 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though one of its 4 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Prescott draws many visitors, but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (8.1%, under the 9.9% cutoff) and its 41 lodging places (0.9 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 7 of its 18 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of Prescott's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
